description: This series is composed of records created or utilized by individual school districts. It is divided into four sub-series. 1. “District Board of Education Records” contains records created or utilized by the boards of education for individual school districts. 2. “School Census Records” contains records of censuses performed at the school district level, 3. “Teachers’ Reports to the Superintendent” are records that document teachers’ names, school names and numbers, subjects taught, programs of study, pupils’ names, ages, attendance and grades, and the condition of school rooms and materials. 4. "Daily Attendance” records are documents created by individual teachers that document student names, classification, attendance, and grades, occasionally.

title: Lyon County Rural School Records
description: This collection contains documents from the rural school system of Lyon County, Iowa dating from 1878-1981. The records cover a majority of the rural schools’ histories, but they are not comprehensive: some records were lost before their transfer to the Center for the History of Rural Iowa Education and Culture. The collection material is arranged into four series -- “County Board of Education, 1883-1975”, “Office of the Superintendent, 1881-1981”, “Township, 1878-1960”, and “District and School, 1882-1966” -- which are sub-divided by format. Series 1. “County Board of Education, 1883-1975” contains records that were created by or utilized by the County Board of Education. Sub-Series 1: Physical Records, 1883-1965 consists of County Board of Education Meeting Minutes, County Board of Education Financial Records, Reorganization and Consolidation Records, Maps, Plat Books, and a small History of Lyon County. Sub-Series 2: Records on Microfilm, 1921-1975 contains County Board of Education Meeting Minutes and Maps of school districts. Series 2. “Office of the Superintendent, 1881-1981” contains records that were created by or utilized by the Superintendent’s Office. Sub-Series 1: Physical Records, 1881-1965 consists of Superintendents’ Secretaries’ Annual Reports, Superintendents’ File, Superintendents’ Cash Book, High School Normal Training Records, Teachers’ Examination Record, Record of Teachers’ Certificates, Teacher Contracts, School Officer and Teacher Records, Educational Directories, Superintendents’ Record of Teachers’ Service, Report of Handicapped Persons to the County Superintendent, Pupil Records, Eighth Grade Examination Records, and Seventh Grade Examination Records. Sub-Series 2: Records on Microfilm, 1881-1981 contains a Superintendents’ Record, High School Normal Training Records, Record of Teacher Attendance and Normal Institute, Teachers’ Examination Records, Record of Teacher Certificates, Teacher/Applicant Record, Teacher Contracts, Office Employee Contracts, Teacher Permanent Cumulative Records, School Officer and Teacher Record, Report of Handicapped Persons to the County Superintendent, City School Enrollment Records and Pupil Lists, Pupils’ Permanent Cumulative Reports, Eighth Grade Examination Records, Eighth Grade Recommendation for Promotion, and Seventh Grade Examination Records. Series 3. “Township, 1878-1960” contains records created by or utilized by the Township Board of Education. Sub-Series 1: Physical Records, 1878-1959 consists of Township Board of Education Meeting Minutes, Township Board of Education Secretaries’ Record, and Township Board of Education Treasurers’ Record. Sub-Series 2: Records on Microfilm, 1878-1960 contains Township Board of Education Secretaries’ Record, Township Board of Education Treasurers’ Record, and a List of Townships and Years of Census Records. Series 4. “District and School, 1882-1966” contains records pertaining to individual school and/or districts. Sub-Series 2: Records on Microfilm, 1882-1966 contains District Board of Education Secretaries’ Record, Room Registers, Teachers’ Reports to the Superintendent, District School Censuses, Preliminary Classification Reports, Daily Attendance Registers, Classification Records, and a History Booklet for Grant Township, School #4. || Boxes 1, 7, 42, and 43 contain and are located with CHRIEC's over-sized material

title: Rough Woods School Collection
description: This collection, dating from 1924-1929, originated from the #3 Rough Woods schoolhouse located in Hardin County, Pleasant Township. Consisting solely of teaching aids known as the "Instructor Picture Series", the Rough Woods School Collection provides insight into the teaching methods utilized in rural schools. The "Instructor Picture Series" encouraged students to think critically about works of art and develop oral and written communication skills in the process.

description: The Jerry and JoAnn Kramer Collection is composed of records dating from 1883-2006 that concern the history of education in Bennington Township, Black Hawk County, Iowa; primarily Bennington Township, #4. Divided into two series, "Series 1: Bennington #4 Renovation Project" and "Series 2: Rural School Records", the collection provides insight into the past and present uses of rural schools. || As avid promoters of Iowa’s cultural heritage, Jerry and JoAnn Kramer are committed to preserving the state’s history for the enjoyment of future generations. This fact is evidenced by their involvement in the restoration of Bennington Township, #4 in Black Hawk County. In 1997, the Bennington Boosters 4-H Club conceived the idea to restore the one-room schoolhouse, which had been in use from 1890-1955. Along with the Bennington Neighborhood Association, the Booster Club formed a non-profit steering committee that oversaw the process. In 2000, the group received a $5,000 grant from the Historic Resource Development Program and completed the restoration in the same year. Due to the tireless efforts of all involved, Bennington Township, #4 is now listed on the National Register of Historic Places. The schoolhouse is currently used by volunteers, such as Mr. and Mrs. Kramer, to inform tour groups of Iowa’s rich educational history. Note written by

title: Aletha Hutchison (Jacobs) Collection
description: The Aletha Hutchison (Jacobs) Collection is composed of materials documenting Hutchison's experiences both as a student and as a teacher in the rural school systems of Iowa and Pennsylvania. The collection includes official school records and Hutchison's personal papers providing insight into many facets of rural school life from 1898-1960. || Born in Buchanan County on July 5, 1884, Aletha Hutchison (Jacobs) attended Homer Township, #3 Mitchell before passing the standard Teachers’ Examination in 1902. After obtaining her teachers certificate, Hutchison (Jacobs) embarked on her teaching career, which would span 58 years, 6 Iowa counties, and 2 states. In the state of Iowa, she taught in Benton County (1900-1902), Buchanan County (1902-1907), Black Hawk County (1912-1916), Grundy County (1916-1920), Wright County (1920-1921), and Webster County (1922). Records indicate that by 1922, she had married Elmer W. Hutchison. This event may have been the reason she left Iowa for Pennsylvania in 1922. The Pennsylvania state school system received 38 years of service from Hutchison (Jacobs) until her retirement in 1960. During her time in Pennsylvania, Hutchison (Jacobs) taught in the following schools: Hummelstown High School in Dauphin County (1922-1924) and Reamstown School in East Cocalico Township, Lancaster County (1926-1960). Despite her death in March 1974, the presence of Hutchison (Jacobs) can still be felt on the educational systems of Iowa and Pennsylvania.

title: Dorothy Mason (Perrin) Textbook Collection
description: Dorothy E. Mason (Perrin) collected a wide range of textbooks used during her time as a student and teacher in Butler County, Iowa. Born on October 32, 1906, to Fred A. Perrin and Elizebeth Schreurs, Dorothy and her sister Esther M. Becker (Perrin) attended Albion Township, #7 Swanton. In 1920, Dorothy graduated and went on to attend New Hartford High School. Following graduation, she enrolled at the Iowa State Teachers College for the 1924-1925 school year. She went on to teach in the New Hartford School District, located in Beaver Township. Many of Dorothy’s textbooks from #7 Swanton were also used by her sister Esther. A 1927 graduate of New Hartford High School, Esther attended Iowa State Teachers College where she received her certificate in 1929. She returned to #7 Swanton where she taught from 1927-1936.

title: Jim Riley Collection on DeSoto Consolidated School
description: The DeSoto Consolidated School possesses a rich history which donor, and former student, Jim Riley is working to preserve. Originally located in Dallas County, Van Meter Township, the DeSoto Consolidated School opened in 1924 and served the children of DeSoto, Iowa, until its closure in 1961. The Jim Riley Collection on DeSoto Consolidated School consists of Mr. Riley's reference files which are in the process of being compiled into a book-length work. From 2013-2014, Mr. Riley corresponded with former students to obtain highlights and memories of their time at DeSoto Consolidated School. Informational sheets, letters, and emails from participating students, teacher lists, written works, and the 2004 publication "Memories: DeSoto Consolidated School Class of 1954" compose the collection.

Wirtz).

title: Des Moines County Rural School Records
description: This collection contains documents from the rural school system of Des Moines County, Iowa dating from 1882-1980. The records cover a majority of the rural schools’ histories, but they are not comprehensive: some records were lost before their transfer to the Center for the History of Rural Iowa Education and Culture. The collection material is arranged into four series: “State of Iowa Department of Public Instruction, 1926-1963”, “County Board of Education, 1919-1969”, “Office of the Superintendent, 1882-1980”, and “District and School, 1891-1965”. Series 1. “State of Iowa Department of Public Instruction, 1926-1963” is comprised of a near-complete run of the Iowa Educational Directory from 1926 to 1963. Series 2. “County Board of Education, 1919-1969” contains records related to the activities of the County Board of Education. This series consists of Annual Financial Reports of Des Moines, Iowa, and Reorganization and Consolidation Records. Series 3. “Office of the Superintendent, 1882-1980” contains records created and kept by the Office of the Superintendent. This series is arranged into three sub-series: 1. “Superintendent’s Financial Records” including administrative finances and library account documents; 2. “Teacher-related Records” including teacher examination and certifications records as well as school officer and teacher directories and registers; and 3. “Pupil-related Records” including censuses, enrollment statistics, and eighth grade examination records. Series 4. “District and School, 1891-1965” contains records created by teachers at the district and school level. These include Room Registers, Teachers’ Reports to the Superintendent, and Daily Attendance Registers.

title: Iowa Cooperative Study of Post High School Education, 1965 - 1967
creator: Board of Directors for the Study of Post High School Education in Iowa
description: This study was organized by the Iowa Association of Private Colleges and Universities, the State Board of Public Instruction, and the State Board of Regents. Its purpose was to reassess each of the Iowan junior colleges’ and Iowan universities’ demographics and how to improve the overall quality of the universities in the state of Iowa. The Board created eight different sub-goals for the study. Separate committees were then assigned: To estimate the size and characteristics of post high school students. (Committee A); To determine the educational needs of post high school students and how to best accommodate them. (Committee B); To determine the areas of research and service which can be used most effectively and efficiently by post high school educational institutions. (Committee C); How to distribute the programs, research and service of post high school. education among the present and future institutions. (Committee D); To determine the facilities needed to accommodate future students and programs. (Committee E); To determine the future staff needs of post high school educational institutions. (Committee F); To discover the best coordination and governance of education beyond high school. (Committee G); and To find methods of financing post high school education. (Committee H). Upon completion of the study, various higher education institutions in Iowa made some changes to their curricula and guiding philosophies. Junior colleges in the state emphasized the integrity of the university and its development and academic freedom. Iowa State University began to offer more majors in scientific fields. The State College of Iowa began to implement more non-teaching programs due to increased enrollment in these areas. || This collection contains the plans, preliminary findings, committee notes, reports, and correspondence from the Iowa Cooperative Study of Post High School Education, which occured from 1965 to 1967. These print documents are a mixture of handwritten, typewritten, official, original, and copied content. Reports include both narrative content and numerical data. Institutions involved in this study were Iowa State University, University of Iowa, State College of Iowa (now the University of Northern Iowa), the Iowa Association of Private Colleges and Universities, the State Department of Public Instruction, and the Board of Regents. Notable State College of Iowa members who contributed to this project were President J. W. Maucker (Chairman) and Dr. Marshall Beard. Once the study was completed it was delivered to the public.

title: Pamphlets in Civics, Iowa State Normal School, no. 1, December 5, 1891
description: This file consists of one, twenty page pamphlet, dated December 5, 1891. It is noted as issue Number 1, though no other issues in this series are known. Included in the pamphlet are texts of early United States documents including the Mayflower Compact; the constitution of the United Colonies of New England; and Penn's Briefe and Plaine Scheam. It also contains various declarations of rights, such as statements by the Congress of 1765 and 1774, and the Virginia convention of May 1776. It is possible that this pamphlet was put together by President Homer Seerley and Professor Leonard Parish, as a precursor to their book, History and Civil Government of Iowa (1897).

title: Official Communications, 1928-1940
description: Latham articulated policies, procedures, and announcements in several series of mimeographed communications. In his Administrative Letters series, Latham informed faculty, administrators, the Board of Education, and others about matters of institutional policy such as use of facilities, requisition of supplies and equipment, travel reimbursement, absences, telephone etiquette, student employment, and faculty classification. His Circular Letters series, sent to the faculty, established policy and distributed news: among the matters treated in these letters are student records, placement of chairs in classrooms, accreditation, the Placement Bureau, telephone service, and assemblies. His Special Announcements series usually told about programs and events such as a visiting speaker. His untitled communications combine many of the functions of the named series noted above.

title: Constantine W. Curris Papers, 1980-2017
creator: Curris, Constantine, 1940-
description: Constantine Curris was born in Lexington, Kentucky, in 1940. He attended the University of Kentucky, where he majored in political science and graduated in 1962. Curris then attended the University of Illinois, earning his master's degree in political science in 1965 before receiving his Ed.D. in higher education from the University of Kentucky. Curris and his wife, Jo, had two children. Curris worked in a variety of higher education administrative positions throughout his career. He first served as vice president and dean of the Midway College (Kentucky) faculty in 1965. Curris became director of academic programs for the West Virginia Board of Education in 1968 before serving as dean of student personnel programs at Marshall University (West Virginia) from 1969-1971. He then spent two years as West Virginia Institute of Technology's vice president and dean of the faculty. In 1973, he was named the president of Murray State University. Curris became president of the University of Northern Iowa in 1983, Curris' goals while leading UNI were "to improve the physical environment of the campus [and] the quality of undergraduate education and student faculty relations." For example, he supported "campus beautification projects," and various buildings were constructed including the business building (later named in his honor), Kamerick Art Building, Roth Apartments, the Center for Energy and Environmental Education, and the Visitor and Information Center. Additionally, under Curris' administration, UNI experienced a rise in enrollment, stronger enrollment requirements, working towards a "comprehensive strategic planning process" for the university as a whole, and a retooling of its General Education program. He also worked "to gain accreditation for business students." Related to this, UNI garnered national attention for its business and education programs. Curris left UNI in 1995 to become president of Clemson University in South Carolina. Outside of his administrative duties, Curris strongly advocated for public higher education and its students, looking at how those fit in the 21st century. He became president of the American Association of State Colleges and Universities in 1999. His professional experiences included membership or leadership roles in: the Kellogg Commission on the Future of State and Land-Grant Universities, the Iowa Board of Economic Development, the Sigma Chi Foundation, and the Iowa Task Force on Teacher Education and Certification. || This relatively small collection contains information about Dr. Curris's information, but little biographical material. title: President's Newsletter and President's Bulletin, 1983-1995

description: The President’s Newsletters for Constantine W. Curris were published between 1985 and 1995. These newsletters were created to provide information on the actions and processes of the Office of the President during these years. The President’s Bulletin was created by UNI President John Joseph Kamerick with the following purposes, as listed in the inaugural Oct. 1, 1970 edition: Provide official policy statements until an updated Faculty Handbook or a policy/procedures book could be written Provide information on various topics When possible, include texts of local, state and national reports affecting education || This collection consists of paper copies of President's Bulletins from the University of Northern Iowa produced from between 1983 and 1995, as well as the Presidential Newsletters written between 1985-1995. The presidential newsletters from 1985-1995 are in the first folder, followed by the 1983-1994 bulletins. There are 31 bulletin folders that exist in chronological order, starting with issue #121 from September 1983 and ending with issue #151 from January, 1994.

title: Founders Day Committee, 1989-1990
creator: Founders Day Committee
description: President Constantine Curris proclaimed April 23, 1990, as Founders Day at the University of Northern Iowa. Founders Day was organized to celebrate the history of UNI amd involvement by the entire campus community was encouraged. The main events of the day were an All-University Convocation and Presidential reception. Speakers at the Convocation included Dr. William Lang, Vice President Emeritus, President Constantine Curris, and Dr. Nancy Marlin, Vice President and Provost. In addition, a historical photo exhibit and multi-image slide show were created and presented honoring the University. Although Founders Day was designated as Monday, April 23, events were scheduled throughout the preceding weekend. They included a musical concert, a film viewing, and a recognition breakfast. Student organizations and students living in residence halls were encouraged to organize their own celebrations in correlation with the larger University celebration. The members of the Founders Day Committee, appointed by President Curris were Thomas Thompson, chair, Walter DeKock, Saul Diamond, Edward Rutkowski, James Skaine, Melba Widmer, and Noreen Hermansen. The committee also hired a cooperative education student, Lynn Arnold, to work as an intern.

title: Robert D. Koob Papers, 1995-2006
creator: Koob, Robert D.
description: Robert Koob was born in Graettinger, Iowa, in 1941. He attended the State College of Iowa (now UNI), majoring in chemistry and graduating in 1962. Koob then taught math and science in Moville, Iowa, before attending the University of Kansas, where he earned his Ph.D. in chemistry. Koob and his wife, Yvonne, had seven children. Koob joined the North Dakota State University (Fargo, ND) faculty in 1967 as an assistant professor of chemistry. While at NDSU, he also served as the vice president for academic affairs and the university's interim president. From 1990-1995, Koob was the senior vice president and vice president for Academic Affairs at California Polytechnic State University. Koob served as the University of Northern Iowa's president from 1995-2006. While he was at UNI, the university's endowment increased by over 100%, enrollment and graduate numbers "reached record levels; and the number of privately funded scholarships increased. Additionally, UNI "had more students benefit from international experience than any other master's-level university in the United States." Koob retired from the UNI presidency in 2006 and returned to California Polytechnic in 2008 as provost and vice president for Academic Affairs, a position in which he served until his retirement in 2012. || Researchers should note that there is some repetition of subject coverage between the contents of the first four boxes and Boxes 5-7. This collection gives a good picture of President Koob's interest in community service and university outreach.

He received his doctorate and master's degree in economics from the University of Illinois and his bachelor's of science degree in business economics from Indiana University. President Allen was vice president for academic affairs and provost at Iowa State University and was responsible to the president in all aspects of the academic programs at Iowa State. He has the distinction of having been named the first University Distinguished Professor in Business at ISU. Before joining the ISU faculty in 1979, he taught at Washington State University and was a Brookings Economic Policy Fellow in the Office of Transportation Regulatory Policy, U.S. Department of Transportation. He was the Visiting McKinley Professor of Economics and Public Utilities at the University of Illinois in 1986-87 and held the Oren Harris Chair in Transportation at the University of Arkansas during the 1990-91 academic year. In 1999 he was appointed chairperson of the committee for the study of Freight Capacity for the Next Century, Transportation Research Board, National Research Council, National Academy of Sciences. In 2007, President Allen was appointed by two state college associations (the American Association of State Colleges and Universities and the National Association of State Universities and Land-Grant Colleges) to the Presidential Advisory Committee for the National Commission of University Accountability. In June 2010, President Allen received a Congressional appointment to serve on the National Advisory Committee on Institutional Quality and Integrity (NACIQI). This committee is required by law to advise the Secretary of Education with respect to establishment and enforcement of the standards of accrediting agencies or associations. Under his leadership, the University of Northern Iowa has established priorities of increasing student achievement in undergraduate programs and providing statewide leadership in Pre-K through 12 education, including UNI's lead role in the Iowa Mathematics and Science Education Partnership with Iowa State University and the University of Iowa. In July 2011, Gov. Branstad and Lt. Gov. Reynolds declared Science, Technology, Engineering and Math (STEM) a priority for our state. Governor Branstad has asked President Allen to serve as co-chair with Lieutenant Governor Reynolds of the STEM Advisory Council. President Allen also co-chairs the Iowa Business Council's Education Excellence in Iowa Roundtable, a non-partisan forum of business and education leaders focused on improving pre-K-16 academic achievement and establishing career development opportunities. He previously co-chaired the Institute for Tomorrow's Workforce, a non-profit educational foundation helping Iowa learners prepare for the global marketplace. A strong supporter of the local community, President Allen is a member of the executive committee of the Greater Cedar Valley Alliance. He and Pat Allen served as co-chairs of the 2010 Cedar Valley United Way Campaign. || This collection consists of speeches, addresses, and remarks by University of Northern Iowa President Benjamin Allen. In a few cases the entire text is present. However, in most cases there is only a detailed outline or a series of talking points. If the occasion for the speech is a building dedication or other formal occasion, the program for that occasion usually accompanies the speech outline. In a few cases, a CD relating to the occasion is present. A few folders contain only an event program and no text. This collection is an excellent resource for researchers who wish to study what the University of Northern Iowa considered to be the most important matters that it wished to bring to public attention at particular points in time. That is, as the leading spokesman for the university, President Allen emphasized issues that he believed were critical to the university's present and future situation. A few speeches reveal a more personal side of President Allen.

title: Malcolm Price Laboratory School Closing; Electronic Mail, 2011-2012
description: In 2012 Malcolm Price Laboratory School was closed. It was later razed. || Following University of Northern Iowa President Benjamin Allen's announcement of the closing of the Malcolm Price Laboratory School and the University Museum, the Waterloo Courier, the Cedar Rapids Gazette, and television station KCRG, requested and received, under open records laws, electronic mail relating to the closings. The electronic mail, about 2200 pages, covers the period from December 1, 2011 through March 7, 2012. The Waterloo Courier printed several articles relating to the electronic mail release, including an article on April 1, 2012, which is included at the head of this collection. The Courier made the electronic mail available in pdf format on its Web site. The mail was divided into six folders: one folder each for University President Benjamin Allen, Provost Gloria Gibson, Dean of the College of Education Dwight Watson, and the University Museum, as well two smaller folders apparently edited to provide easy access by Courier readers. The Rod Library Information Technologies Department downloaded the files. The Special Collections and University Archives Division printed them out. The printouts are arranged as they appeared in the pdf folders. This collection offers a perspective on the thoughts and considerations of university administrators as they came to their decisions. It also provides a look at campus and community reactions to those decisions.

title: North Central Association, Higher Learning Commission Re-accreditation Visit Collection, 2008-2011
creator: Self Study Committee
description: This collection was assembled in preparation for a re-accreditation visit to the University of Northern Iowa by the North Central Association, Higher Learning Commission in November 2010. As such, the collection is an excellent snapshot of the programs, services, plans, websites, and policies of the university at that time. In addition, the official university publications included in the collection offer a good look at the way in which the university wished to be viewed by the public and the accreditors. Most of this collection served as a body of evidence and support for the self-study performed in preparation for the visit of the accreditation team. Over half of the collection is arranged as supporting documentation for the footnotes and references in the self-study. Files are labeled and arranged in the order in which footnotes or references appear in the self-study: for example, Chapter 1, footnotes 1-10; Chapter 1, footnotes 11-20; and so on. In most footnotes folders, the actual referenced document is present. In a few cases, there is only a further reference to a source. The collection also includes some freestanding documents that were apparently assembled for the use of the accreditation visitors. There is also a limited amount of evidence of the work of the campus preparation committee itself.

title: Center for the Enhancement of Teaching Files, 1991-2002
creator: University of Northern Iowa. Center for the Enhancement of Teaching
description: In accordance with a recommendation for the University Faculty Senate, Vice President and Provost Nancy Marlin created the Center for the Enhancement of Teaching. G. Roger Sell was hired as Director of the Center. He began work in January 1993. After his arrival, Professor Sell conducted a needs assessment for the Center. He then developed a program of services to meet the needs of faculty who wished to improve and expand their teaching capabilities. The services included seminars, surveys, broad studies of problem areas, guest appearances by notable teachers, short papers on a variety of topics, and studies on many issues involving teaching and learning. The services focused on assisting new faculty, strengthening the Humanities sequence and the Capstone course, and developing faculty teaching capabilities. The Center ended operations when Professor Sell took a position at Southwest Missouri State University in 2002. || These files offer a very good picture of the programs and services offered by the Center for the Enhancement of Teaching. The files include Professor Sell's short papers in the improvement of teaching, documentation of the many programs that the Center offered, and strong collections relating to the Qualities of an Educated Person project and Student Outcomes Assessment.

title: Classic Upward Bound Collection, 2017
creator: Classic Upward Bound
description: Classic Upward Bound (CUB) is a program that prepares high school students for success in college. It is funded by both the United States Department of Education and the University of Northern Iowa. CUB's purpose "...is to promote students' awareness of the possibility of furthering their education beyond high school and to help students become more aware of their self-worth, uniqueness, culture, and individual creativity." At UNI, students who have finished 8th grade or in in 9th-11th grades from the Waterloo Community School District may apply for CUB. Two-thirds of program applicants must come from low-income and first-generation college families. Program participants are involved in many activities such as recreational, cultural, and educational opportunities, as well as spending six weeks during the summer at UNI, living in dorms and taking classes to help strengthen their academics. || This collection consists of one invitation to the 2017 Annual Classic Upward Bound Banquet.

title: Certificates and Diplomas, 1871-1935
creator: University of Northern Iowa
description: This collection of material consists primarily of certificates and diplomas used by the University of Northern Iowa to signify the completion of courses of study. There are also a few diplomas and certificates from other institutions and government agencies. First, there are diplomas and certificates that were actually issued to particular students. Most of these documents drifted into the University Archives one-by-one, or as parts of small alumni collections, over the years. These documents are in Boxes 1 and 5. The collection also includes diplomas and certificates that were never issued. Many of these documents are blank, some are spoiled or defective, and some are signed completely or in part by school authorities. A few have names of particular students entered on them. Perhaps these documents were defective in some way or perhaps these students did not finish their courses of study. There are multiple copies of many of these documents. Some of these documents, especially the early ones, are large and handsome, with calligraphic embellishment. The early documents are also interesting in that they include the signatures of the entire faculty and the governing board of the institution. There is a small collection of diploma cases in Box 4.

title: Entrance examination grade books, 1875-1945
description: In the first two volumes, 1876-1893 and 1893-1911, are found each student's name (entered alphabetically), the student's age, his/her grade average, the names of the exams taken, and the exam grades received. The exams were taken each term with Term I being the Fall Term and Term II being the Spring Term. The names are entered by Class A, B, C, etc. within each term. Beginning with the 1886 Fall Term, the exam date for each student was entered as well as remarks related to individual students (county appointing each student, assignment, etc.) Toward the back of the first volume are the enrollment figures for the various terms as well as for the entire year. Indication is made as to whether of not the student had either an undergraduate of a graduate grade card. Starting with the 1907 Summer Term, birth dates are included as well. In the volume dated 1911-1919 are lists of students interviewed in the Fall, 1911 including credits by examination (either passed of failed). Students' names do not seem to follow and logical order. This is true of the volume dated 1919-1945 as well.
publisher: University Archives || University of Northern Iowa

title: Project V.I.P. Records, 1995-2004
creator: Project V.I.P. (Volunteers are Important People)
description: Project V.I.P. (Volunteers are Important People) was a student-run organization founded circa 1997 at the University of Northern Iowa. In its early years, it was a collaboration among the Department of Residence, Career Student Services, and the Student Organization Center. Project V.I.P.’s main goal was to “promote volunteerism” among the UNI campus community. Project V.I.P. partnered with the Volunteer Center of Cedar Valley to connect with over 75 non-profit organizations. The Volunteer Fair, coordinated by Project V.I.P. and the Office of Experiential Learning, allowed students, faculty, and staff to interact with volunteer organizations’ representatives and learn about volunteer opportunities in the Cedar Falls and Waterloo area. Project V.I.P. was last mentioned as sponsoring volunteer fairs in 2004. However, as of December 2019, volunteer fairs are still organized at UNI. || This collection dates from 1995-2004 and contains materials primarily related to Project V.I.P.’s administrative and promotional tasks. Included are logistical and planning documents for the 1998 and 2000 volunteer fairs, which consist of checklists, flyers, brochures, registration forms, correspondence, set-up and sign-in sheets, lists of participating non-profits and more. Many of the materials contain handwritten annotations. Also included are Project V.I.P. Coordinator position descriptions and information and year-end reports. Items of note: 1995 proposal to establish a UNI Volunteers are Important People Center 2002 U.S. House of Representatives certificate offering congressional recognition of Project V.I.P.’s work, signed by then-Iowa congressman Jim Nussle. || The collection is arranged chronologically.

title: Contracts, Agreements, Leases, and Insurance Claims, 1965-1990
creator: University of Northern Iowa
description: This series is a collection of contracts, agreements, leases, and insurance claims relating to the operations of the University of Northern Iowa and its facilities. The series contains information relating to the fires that destroyed Central Hall in 1965 and Old Gilchrist Hall in 1972. There is also documentation of the series of problems relating to the KUNI broadcasting tower in the late 1970s and the installation of equipment in the new Power Plant in 1979-1980. While some files are quite small, many files contain extensive material such as insurance loss claims, correspondence, and legal documentation of contentious issues. The material is arranged in an order very similar to that in which it was received.

title: Sunset Village / Quonset Hut Register, 1946-1948
description: Sunset Village and its quonset huts were built in 1946 following the end of World War II, with the main goal to provide housing for veterans and their families. The Iowa State Teachers College (later UNI) “acquired 45 quonset huts from the Regional Federal Public Housing Authority and then expended $40,000 to put in sewer, water, and other utilities.” The quonset huts were shipped from Oregon and were located on Highway 57 across from campus, at the end of College Street. Each hut could accommodate two families and military families were given first priority. The huts were ready for occupants in October 1946 and by Fall 1947, units could accommodate 114 students, with all but 18 reserved for veterans. The village continued to grow, with the possibility of housing 138 families in the 72 quonset and barrack-style huts. Rent initially ranged from $20-$33 per month and later, was $25/month and $40/month. These rates were cheaper than those at South Courts mobile homes and Hillside Courts. According to William Lang, “the quonset huts of Sunset Village provided cheap but substandard housing for veterans’ families…” Indeed, there were a few problems with the quonsets, including inadequate heating and their overall issue as a fire hazard. The university announced in Summer 1970 that the Sunset Village units would be gradually phased out as vacancies occurred. In Fall 1971, with Hillside Courts nearing completion, Sunset Village residents were given the option of moving to the new apartments or staying in Sunset Village until Spring 1972. Sunset Village officially closed in August 1972 after which the university attempted to sell the buildings. Ultimately, only three were sold, with some kept for a number of years as storage space and art studios. The remainder of the buildings were razed. || This collection consists of a 152 page bound notebook, dating from 1946-1948. It consists of entries noting when specific people and their families moved in and/or out; whether the unit was furnished; occasional notes about damage (see page 6); and street names for units, such as E. title: Campanile Committee Records, 1923-1946
creator: University of Northern Iowa. Campanile Committee
description: The Campanile Committee was responsible for leading fundraising efforts to build the Campanile. The committee also had some responsibilities for Campanile upkeep and improvement after it was built. Among the most important documents in this series are the Fasoldt correspondence and the letter from James Owen Perrine. In the Fasoldt correspondence, Dudley Fasoldt writes at length about the Fasoldt clock mechanism that was originally mounted in the Campanile. J. O. Perrine, in his 1946 letter to I. H. Hart, writes about what he believed to be his pivotal role in the acquisition of the clock mechanism. There are also important exchanges of correspondence between Teachers College officials and the architects of Proudfoot, Bird, and Rawson on the design and construction of the Campanile.

description: This series is a collection of Alumni Association documents developed over the years by Alumni Association staff. title: Filing system code for Information Systems and Computer Services, 1991
description: Note to researchers: This filing system code accompanied the collection when it arrived in the University Archives. The individual elements of the code consist of two letters and a number, such as A4A, B6L, or L7B. The code is a hierarchical system that mirrors the administrative organization chart of the university. Many of the folder tabs in this collection included this code. When that code appeared on the original folder, the records processor included the code on the new folder. However, the collection itself was not in anything approaching coded arrangement when it arrived in the Archives. Nor did every folder include a coded notation; many folders were labeled "Miscellaneous". In addition, much of the collection had been developed long after the last revision to the filing system codes. Consequently, the records processor imposed his own order on the collection, though with some reference to the apparent original order. Researchers may wish to consult the 1991 filing guide to get a clearer sense of the contents of some of the folders.

title: Manuals and Catalogues - Educational Media Center - Center for Educational Technology, 1949-1991
creator: University of Northern Iowa. Educational Media Center
description: The University of Northern Iowa's Educational Media Center was a campus-wide organization created to facilitate learning through providing faculty with media and equipment to help them in the classroom. The organization created informational booklets beginning in 1949, branched out to create Curriculum Laboratory informational booklets and catalogues in 1959, and started creating multi-media catalogues in 1972. These materials were published until 1992, when the organization became the Center for Educational Technology. || This series is a collection of information booklets about the Curriculum Laboratory’s audio-visual services, multimedia catalogues from the Educational Media Center, and other information booklets about the Educational Media Center, such as the faculty handbook and annual summary. The purpose of the Curriculum Laboratory booklets was to inform people about the audio and visual services located there, and to make students aware that they were welcome to use those services. The multimedia catalogues include the collection of tapes, film, and other forms of media available for checkout at the Curriculum Laboratory; an index of the titles of those pieces in the media collection and their producers. || This collection is arranged chronologically.

title: Board of Student Publications, 1932-1992
creator: University of Northern Iowa. Board of Student Publications
description: The Board of Student Publications, as it was originally called, has had a variety of names over the years. It was renamed the Board of Control of Student Publications in the 1934-1935 school year before reverting to the Board of Student Publications during the 1935-1936 academic year. In 1936-1937, it became the Board of Control. The next documented minutes are from the 1948-1949 school year, when the organization was called the Board of Control of Student Publications. In 1972-1973 the name was changed again to the Board of Student Publications. || The school years 1932-1933, where the collection begins, through 1938-1939 are documented only by minutes. There is no documentation for the years 1939-1940 through 1942-1943. Financial records are the organization’s only documentation from 1943-1944 through 1947-1948. After that the documentation is very strong on minutes through 1991-1992. Most years between 1948-1949 and 1961-1962 have financial and personnel documentation. The school year 1961-1962 was the first to retain documents of policies, constitutions, and by-laws. Most years thereafter did, as well. In the 1968-1969 school years documents began to be retained for correspondence, proposals, specifications, recommendations, and requisitions for equipment. From 1968-1969 through 1991-1992 the documentation is strong in each area. Included in the 1982 documents is information from the Associated Collegiate Press and National Council.

title: Kudos, 1998-2016
creator: University of Northern Iowa. Office of Public Relations
description: This series consists of printouts of Kudos that appeared online. Kudos was an Office of Public Relations publication which acknowledged those faculty and staff members who had recently or soon would be published; those who recently presented papers, lectures, and exhibitions; and those who won awards and honors. Kudos was first published as a permanent section of the Campus News Network (CNN) newsletter in 1990. At some point the section was expanded to an insert included with the CNN newsletter once or twice a month. In April 1998, the Office of Public Relations began publishing Kudos only online and discontinued the page in 2008. Afterward, the College of Social and Behavioral Sciences (CSBS) continued publishing Kudos in its newsletter, but only for faculty and staff in that department. Special Collections maintains an index to Kudos, which is found in the reading room. Kudos from 1990-March 1998 are indexed with the CNN Kudos from 1998-2008 are included in this box, along with 2009-2016 issues of the CSBS newsletter.

title: United Faculty records, publications, and papers, 1969-2013
description: This collection consists of master agreements, correspondence, negotiation documents, United Faculty Presidents' notebooks, arbitration records, grievance records, reports, meeting minutes, newsletters, and audio cassette tapes documenting the history of UNI's faculty labor union, United Faculty (UF). Many of these records document the process of negotiating new collective bargaining agreements with the University, including research conducted by UF, proposals, and arbitration proceedings between the Univerisy and UF. Also documented are the non-negotiating activities of the union over the years, such as the constitution and bylaws, promotional materials and FAQs, surveys and reports on working conditions, meeting minutes of the executive board and the board of the Iowa Higher Education Association (IHEA), and administrative papers. Individual grievance and arbitration records are restricted, while those invlolving the union itself are available to researchers. || United Faculty (UF) is a labor union representing faculty at the University of Northern Iowa. Formed in 1975 through a merger between the American Association of University Professors (AAUP) and the Iowa Higher Education Association (IHEA), it was elected in 1976 as the sole representative of faculty for purposes of collective bargaining.

title: Correspondence, 1957-2009
description: Series 1, Correspondence, 1957-2009, consists of Gilgen's incoming and outgoing correspondence with various individuals and organizations. Materials include handwritten and typed letters, emails, and postcards. The correspondence covers many subjects, with the bulk concerned with Gilgen's publications and research, ranging from journal articles to book manuscripts. Other letters focus on his time as a Fulbright-Hays lecturer (1971-1972) at University College Galway, including his family's passport photographs; a handful of letters related to joining the UNI faculty in 1973; 50th anniversary materials for Garfield High School's Golden Anniversary (Akron, OH); and early 1990s correspondence concerning the Clinton administration's health care reform efforts in relation to the field of psychology. The majority of this series is business and professional-related with a small amount of personal content. This series is arranged chronologically.
publisher: University Archives || University of Northern Iowa

title: Administrative Records
description: The Administrative Records series is broken up into two categories. The first is comprised of department minutes which include topics such as graduate students; curriculum and courses; committee work; the department's budgets; promotions and tenure; department events; faculty hirings; and departmental student employees. A majority of the minutes are typed, with some containing handwritten annotations. Also included are a few handwritten notes from assorted department meetings. These materials span 1973-1993 and are arranged chronologically by academic year. The second grouping in the Administrative Records series consists of the department's General Correspondence & Documents, ranging from 1985 to 1993. A variety of topics are covered including discussions of courses and curriculum requirements; salary and financial information; administrative and strategic goals for the broader College of Social & Behavioral Sciences; notes from Department Head meetings; reports; a few minutes from the CSBS faculty senate meetings; and schedules/itineraries from the interview process for potential hires. These materials are arranged chronologically by academic year.

title: Programs & Ephemera
description: The second series, Programs & Ephemera, 1969-2017, includes brochures, fliers, memoranda, and announcements for various meetings and lectures either sponsored or co-sponsored by the Department of Political Science. The lectures featured both regional and national speakers, such as Iowa governor Terry Branstad, Sargent Shriver, and Walter Mondale. Also included is information about the Iowa Consortium for the Social Studies and announcements regarding department faculty position openings. These materials are arranged chronologically.

title: Sheet music, 1892-2005
description: Arranged alphabetically by title, followed by the year of publication. || Dr. Waack donated an extensive collection of sheet music to Special Collections. These range in date from 1892 to 2005, the bulk of which were published in the 1920s and 1940s. The piano/vocal scores consist of popular songs of the times, movie and Broadway show tunes, hymns, patriotic songs from both World Wars, and a few piano pieces in the more classical vein. Because many of the songs were published before Dr. Waack was born, it is believed this music may have been owned by his mother or grandmother.

title: Dean's Office files, 1949-2006
creator: University of Northern Iowa. College of Natural Sciences
description: The collection is wide-ranging. It includes speeches by Deans Roy H. Saigo and Gerald W. Intemann as well as records of several committees in which the Dean of the College of Natural Sciences had a particular interest. There is also good information about some of the early organizational plans for the college administrative structure, shortly after the college was organized. Probably the strongest point of this collection is the material relating to the design, construction, renovation, and use of facilities for departments and programs in the College of Natural Sciences: namely, the Science Building (later McCollum Science Hall), the Industrial Technology Center, Wright Hall, Latham Hall, and the Center for Energy and Environmental Education. Material relating to the original construction of and later additions to McCollum Science Hall is especially detailed. The collection is also strong in documenting the development and early years of the Doctor of Industrial Technology degree in the Department of Industrial Technology. There is also an excellent fifty-year run of correspondence and reports outlining the involvement of the University of Northern Iowa with the Iowa Lakeside Laboratory.

title: School of Music programs, 1985-2019
creator: University of Northern Iowa. School of Music
description: Music has been a subject at the University of Northern Iowa since its founding in 1876. Now part of the College of Humanities and Fine Arts, music was initially offered alongside art in the Art Department. This arrangement lasted until 1892, when the two subject areas split, and music became the Vocal and Instrumental Music Department. This name lasted until 1896, when the department name switched to the broader Music Department. The Music Department experienced fairly frequent name changes in the early 20th century. In 1909, it split into four distinct divisions: the Public School Music Department, Orchestral and Band Music Department, Pianoforte Music Department, and the Voice Department. By 1911, however, there were just two music departments, the Music Department and the Violin, and Orchestral and Band Music Department. Over the next few years, department name changes included the Orchestral Music Department, and shifts between the Music Department to the Public School Music Department, and back again. By 1934, the two different music departments at the time, the Orchestral Music Department and the Music/Public School Music faculty merged to form the single Music Department. The final name change came in 1978, when the department was renamed the School of Music. || This collection consists of School of Music programs for a variety of events including student, studio, and faculty recitals, ensemble concerts, and guest artist performances. It dates from 1985-present. Specific events include All-State, Chimes of Christmas, the Tallcorn Jazz Festival, and the Faculty Artist Showcase. The collection also contains web content captured using the web archiving tool, Archive-It. To view this content, please visit the Concert Program web archive. Represented ensembles include (but are not limited to) Jazz Bands I and III, Jazz Panthers, UNI Chamber Singers, Symphonic Band, Wind Symphony, Concert Band, New Horizons Band, the Symphony Orchestra, UNI Singers, Women's Chorus, and the Varsity Men's Glee Club. || The collection is arranged chronologically by academic year.

title: "Songs in the Air" radio program collection
creator: Mitchell, John
description: The "Songs in the Air" radio program was produced by the Iowa State Teachers College (ISTC) radio studios and began circa 1948, lasting until at least 1958. The fifteen minute program was broadcast every Monday on the WOI Ames radio station. It was conducted by ISTC music professor John Mitchell, with the goal of teaching "rote songs" to Iowa elementary students. ISTC students sometimes participated in the program as studio singers, helping to lead the listeners in singing. In August 1949, ISTC radio director Herbert V. Hake noted that the program "received excellence response" the previous year. Audiences ranged from 15,000-25,000 school children in 88 Iowa counties, roughly 3,000 classrooms, and six surrounding states. The program appealed to rural schools where music classes were not as robust as those in cities. || This collection contains three ISTC "Songs in the Air" study guides. Each contains a number of songs, complete with musical scoring and lyrics, as well as copyright and publishing information for a majority of the songs. Of note is that Herbert Hake provided illustrations for the study guides, including the 1949-1950 guide in this collection.

title: G.S. Robinson letter, October 24, 1916
description: Gifford Simeon Robinson was born in Tremont, Illinois, on May 28, 1843. He served in the Civil War, during which he was seriously wounded at the Battle of Chickamauga. After the war he studied law at Washington University in St. Louis, graduating in 1869. He moved to Storm Lake, Iowa, in 1870 and set up a law practice. He was later elected to the Iowa House of Representatives, serving from 1876-1878. From 1882-1886 he was an Iowa state senator, and from 1888-1899 a justice on the Iowa Supreme Court. Three of those years were spent as Chief Justice. After leaving the court he was appointed to the Iowa Board of Control, serving in that capacity from 1900-1913. Mr. Robinson died on his 93rd birthday, May 28, 1936. || This box contains one typewritten letter from G.S. Robinson to Professor David Sands Wright, dated October 24, 1916, in response to Professor Wright's request for information about the early history of Iowa State Normal School.

title: Charles Ernest Hearst materials / Hearst family biographical information
description: Series 1, the Charles E. Hearst materials, consists of records created and used by Charles E. Hearst, as well as biographical information and other documents related to the Hearst family as a whole. The materials created by Charles E. Hearst include notes about agricultural issues, records from the Maplehearst family farm, and his work in passing agricultural legislation. The bulk of his records consist of his personal and professional correspondence. Some of this correspondence has been photocopied due to the originals' fragility and deteriorating condition. Most of the correspondence written to and from Hearst were written during his term as the Iowa Farm Bureau president from 1924 to 1935. The correspondence, and his records in general, reflect the range of problems which farms and agriculture faced during the 1920s and 1930s. The correspondence also related to Hearst's work shepherding legislation through the Iowa legislature and United States Congress, including the Mc-Nary Haugen Bill and the Agricultural Adjustment Administration of the New Deal. Other types of materials in the Charles E. Hearst series include news releases, American Farm Bureau Federation circulars, position statements from various agricultural organizations, and ephemeral agricultural publications. The remainder of the Charles E. Hearst series includes a handful of items created by other Hearst family members, photographs of the Hearst family and farm, and news clippings.

title: Charles Joseph Hearst and Gladys Henderson Hearst materials
description: The Charles Joseph Hearst and Gladys Henderson Hearst series contains materials related to both Charles Joseph and Gladys. Gladys Henderson Hearst's files consist of documents related to and representative of her time in the Women's Accepted for Voluntary Emergency Service (WAVES) during World War II. Types of materials include papers and photographs. The photographs are a combination of the WAVES training program at the Iowa State Teachers College (now the University of Northern Iowa) and nationally. Many include types and handwritten captions. The Russia trip materials consist of news clippings related to an agricultural exchange between the United States and the Soviet Union in 1955. Charels Joseph Hearst was part of the American delegation that visited the Soviet Union. These materials were likely collected by Charles or Gladys. Note: Charles Joseph Hearst's personal papers are held at Iowa State University.

title: [The Running of Widows - Sewell Becker] typescript
description: Unpublished typescript with editorial marks by James Hearst. 178 pages plus 2 pages of story outline. No date. This typescript seems to be a draft of a novel or series of short stories. The assumed title of this typescript, The running of widows, is simply the name given at the top of the first page of the first chapter. The remaining chapters are titled by the name of the character featured in that particular chapter. The first chapter sets the theme for the work: ten widows, of considerably different circumstances, organize themselves into a mutual assistance network. Each of the remaining chapters tells the story of one widow's life. The individual chapters of this typescript seem to be fairly well-developed. And there are relationships and references between and among the chapters. But there does not seem to be a resolution, summary, or conclusion to the collection.

title: Publications log, 1960s - 1984
description: 1. One large set of logs was kept in three 7 inch by 9 inch ring binders. The binders were discarded during the processing of the collection, because they were badly deteriorated. The pages from each binder were then transferred into individual file folders, one folder per binder. Nearly all of the pages in the binders consist of typed copies of James Hearst's poems. But in a few cases, instead of a typed copy of a poem, there is a clipped copy from the original publication, or a photocopy of the original publication, glued to the page. In nearly all cases, there are bibliographic citations to the publication(s) in which a poem appeared, written or typed at the bottom of each page. The overall arrangement of the three binders is chronological, according to the time of the first appearance of a poem in print. However, there are significant departures from this order, especially in folders one and two. The binders also include a few poems that are noted as "unpublished." Meryl Norton Hearst was likely responsible for maintaining this log. Binder 1--mostly 1960s, but with some exceptions on either side Binder 2--mostly 1970s, but with some early work Binder 3--1979-1984 2. Spiral notebook arranged alphabetically by first word of a poem's title, with citations to publications in which the poem appeared 3. Note card file, 3 X 5 inches, arranged alphabetically by first word of a poem's title, with citations to publications in which the poem appeared

title: James Hearst incoming and outgoing correspondence
description: James Hearst's correspondence comprises the majority of this series. It contains approximately 1000 incoming and outgoing letters, which are a mix of personal and professional topics and correspondents, such as with Hearst's first and second wives, friends, publishers, discussions about his writing, his employment at the University of Northern Iowa (UNI), and much more. One of Hearst's most frequent correspondents was UNI president James William Maucker, who often signed off his letters as "Bill." Other notable correspondents include Ferner Nuhn, Bess Streeter Aldrich, Robert Frost, Carl Sandburg, and Jesse Stuart. Also included are letters from United States Vice President H.A. Wallace; one letter from former First Lady Eleanor Roosevelt to Carmelita Hearst (August 21, 1951); and one letter from Randolph Hearst (May 22, 1974). Some of the correspondence is addressed to Carmelita Hearst, James Hearst's first wife, and Meryl Norton Hearst, his second wife. There are also many letters between Hearst and editors, publishers, and presses discussing his work and publications. There is a name index to most correspondents available in the University Archives and digitally. "T.L.S." means Typed Letter Signed. "A.L.S." means autograph letter signed. This index was updated to include newly-processed material March 2017.Physical copies of the updated index are available by request. A date, a name, or a portion thereof within parentheses () indicates that the information was added on the basis of the processor's knowledge or information from an envelope.

title: "ISTC 50 Anniversary Dream Season, 1960 - 2010" and "ISTC Panthers Anniversary Dream Season, 1960-2020" by Warren Reyerson, 2010, 2020
creator: Reyerson, Warren
description: Warren Reyerson created this booklet as a way to commemorate the 1960 football season and team at Iowa State Teachers College, now the University of Northern Iowa. Warren Reyerson's father, Mace Reyerson, was a member of the 1960 team. Warren Reyerson distributed copies of this booklet to members of that team, which was inducted into the Athletics Hall of Fame at the University of Northern Iowa in 2015. In 1960, the Panther football team completed a perfect regular season with a 9-0 record and an appearance in the Mineral Water Bowl in Excelsior Springs, Missouri. || This series consists of a PDF booklet created by Warren Reyerson celebrating the 1960 Iowa State Teachers College football team. The booklet is titled "ISTC 50 Anniversary Dream Season, 1960 - 2010," and was intended to be a gift to the 1960 team. The booklet contains photographs, artwork, and text about the 1960 season and the 50th anniversary reunion for this team, which was held in September 2010. Text includes information about individual players, game narratives and statistics, rosters, schedules, and general memories. The series also includes a physical copy of an updated version of the booklet honoring the team's 60th anniversary.

title: Correspondence; College Printed Material; Teaching and Mentoring Materials; Music Programs; Materials Related to Her Family; Miscellaneous Material; History of Coon Rapids, Iowa; Photographs
description: Correspondence All letters are arranged chronologically, regardless of correspondent and recipient. In most instances the envelope has been discarded, unless it was needed to establish a date. There are some letters that are not dated and had no envelope, but because of the correspondent, writing style, age of the paper, and / or current events mentioned, it was possible to determine the decade. These are filed at the beginning of the folder containing that decade. The correspondence dates from long before Miss Middleton was born—a teacher evaluation of one of her ancestors in 1859 is the first—and continues until just before her death in 2015. A majority of the correspondence in this box is of a professional nature, relating to her career in teaching, writing, and curriculum development, or letters from past students and teachers thanking her for her influence upon their lives. However, many personal letters can also be found here, from her father Otis, her sister Beth, her mother Maude, other relatives, and her myriad of friends. Oddly, there is very little from or about her sister Vera, who, but for a photograph, a high school graduation card, and three or four brief newspaper clippings from the 1930s or 1940s, virtually disappears from Miss Middleton’s records after 1920. Note: Box 4 also contains correspondence, which Miss Middleton had pasted into scrapbooks. Much of this is personal, such as cards and letters from friends and colleagues celebrating her retirement and 90th, 95th, and 100th birthdays. Pre-1900 1900-1909 1910-1919 1920-1929 1930-1939 1940-1949 1950-1959 1960-1969 1970-1979 1973-2007 – Correspondence with H. Roger Grant 1980-1989 1990-1999 2000-2015 Undated College Printed Material One file with primarily college programs, but also reunion material. Arranged chronologically. Teaching and Mentoring Materials Spelling lists and other educational material, as well as brochures and handouts pertaining to mentoring programs. Unsorted. Music Programs Programs from musical events spanning several decades for which Miss Middleton served as piano accompanist. Arranged chronologically. Miscellaneous Material Material that didn’t easily fit into other categories. Unsorted. Photographs Many photographs came to us in photo albums. The pages were removed from three of the albums and put into folders in the same order as Miss Middleton had arranged them. There were two photo albums from which the pages were not removed for fear of causing damage. These albums were too large for our regular boxes and are kept with oversized material in Box 4. In addition, Box 4 contains two smaller photo albums. Also, over a hundred loose photographs were interspersed throughout the collection. These have been gathered together and put in protective plastic sleeves. However, there was no attempt to arrange them into any systematic order. title: Scrapbooks
description: Series 3, Scrapbooks, consists of three items. Scrapbook 1 largely documents Sucher's 1934 trip to England with the Campus Playboys and includes photographs of well-known tourist sites and the group aboard the ship, Carinthia. Additionally, photocopied scrapbook pages feature family, family homes in Cedar Falls, band concerts, and more. Most of the photographs are captioned. Scrapbook 2 is titled, "4-H Club Activities of Richard Sucher" and has two sections. First is a set of pages from September 1924 with handwritten notes and typewritten correspondence about caring for a calf in relation to Sucher's club participation. The rest of the scrapbook dates from 1924 to 1929 and details Sucher's involvement in 4-H and the Black Hawk County Dairy Calf Club program. Included are photographs and information about Richard; letters of recommendation; news clippings; certificates of merit; correspondence about Dairy Calf Club judging, and a handwritten narrative of Sucher's club activities. This portion of the scrapbook also contains captioned photographs of the club. Scrapbook 3 consists of ephemeral content from Sucher and the Campus Playboys' 1934 England trip. Included is a Cunard-Anchor Line contract; Cunard ephemera such as luggage tags and schedules; postcards; coasters; menus; and more. Additionally, there are matchbooks, hotel information and British sightseeing booklets, and hostel receipts.

title: Gender and vocational choices of male elementary school teachers
description: Two areas of special interest for Professor Nielsen were: Character education and the vocational choices of male elementary school teachers. He studied the subjects, conducted research, participated in meetings relating to the topics, implemented programs at the Malcolm Price Laboratory School, presented his research at professional meetings, and wrote on these topics. In the process of his work, Professor Nielsen accumulated a substantial body of information on these subjects. Because these were areas of special interest for Professor Nielsen, the processor of this collection retained most of the secondary material that Professor Nielsen collected. This secondary material includes professional articles, newspaper clippings, and program descriptions that reflect a wide range of views. This collection also contains some material written by Professor Nielsen himself on these topics.

title: Censorship Clippings file, 1970-2004
description: The general material relating to national issues is arranged alphabetically by the name of the article or subject. The general Iowa material is arranged chronologically, for the most part. The specific Iowa cases are arranged alphabetically by the name of the city in which the case took place. These files were created by Professor Lucille Lettow, Youth Collection Librarian at the University of Northern Iowa. Professor Barbara Safford also added material to these files. The files consist primarily of newsclippings and photocopies of articles relating to censorship, book challenges, and intellectual freedom. Some of the files relate to cases in which Professor Lettow assisted libraries and librarians when they faced challenges to their book selections. In these cases there are sometimes E-mail messages relating to Professor Lettow's assistance. The collection is divided into three parts: national issues and cases; general Iowa concerns; and specific Iowa cases.

creator: Access Services / Circulation staff
description: This scrapbook consists of various ephemeral materials compiled by the Rod Library Circulation (now Access Services) staff, largely from the 1970s to early 1980s. Included are examples of day-to-day unit operations, such as "book missing" cards and reading room slips with patron information, call numbers, and book information. title: Museum Administrative files, c. 1983-2012
creator: UNI Museum
description: The University of Northern Iowa (UNI) Museum traces its early roots to the 1890s, when a “Cabinet of Natural History” was created for instructional purposes in a campus science laboratory. Early collections focused on Geology, Zoology, and Native American artifacts. The UNI Museum has been located in a few different spots on UNI’s campus throughout its history, including the Administration Building, Seerley Hall, the Physical Plant Shops, and its Hudson Road location. It is currently located in Rod Library. It has been part of the Biology Department, Field Services Division, and the Division of University Relations and Development before its inclusion in the Rod Library administration. The Museum provides educational opportunities and programming for the campus and Cedar Valley community. It has four collecting areas: BIology, Geology, History, and World Cultures/Anthropology, as well as overseeing the Rural Schools Collection and the Marshall Center School. || The UNI Museum administrative files consist of materials related to various aspects of running and managing the Museum. It includes correspondence among Glen Hansen, Jim Bodensteiner, Kent Johnson, and Sue Grosboll concerning building repairs and renovations; accreditation files; annual reports dating from 2003-2010; a file of survey material from former UNI Museum Director Ronald Wilson’s survey of UNI Faculty to inform the Museum’s five year plan; Friends of the UNI Museum information; and more. Please see the inventory for a complete list.

Swain. Slides in this set can be matched to the indexes within the above publications. The slides were available for purchase and use by educational institutions. The series information was derived and matched from the catalogs.

title: “Some Incidents in the Life of J.F. Reed” (student account of life at Iowa State Normal School), c. 1885
description: Reed’s obituary from the Ames Milepost, January 1939: J. F. Reed, former Story county resident, but for many years a resident of Minnesota, died … at Canby, Minn. Friday and the body was brought to Nevada for funeral services and burial by the side of the wife who passed away a number of years ago. He leaves one son Jeff Reed who lives in the west, and a daughter Mrs. Joyce Cornell of Canby, Minn. at whose home he died. Mr. Reed, a son of an Illinois Grove pioneer family was born northeast of Zearing, received his education in the schools of the county, later had some college work, served two terms as county superintendent of schools in the early '90s, represented Story county in the lower house of the 26th General Assembly and a special session; shortly afterwards went into the Federal service, moved to Minneapolis and had lived in Minnesota the most of the time since. Besides his son and daughter, he leaves brothers Ed and Clay Reed of Zearing, Claude Reed of Eldora and Frank Reed whose whereabouts are unknown here. Mr. Reed visited Zearing friends and relatives a few months ago and during that time was in Nevada for few hours greeting old friends. || John Frederick Reed (October 17, 1863-January 26, 1939), called Fred, wrote this account of his life from memory, then he and his daughter Joyce checked the notes for date accuracy and made corrections. The full manuscript is entitled Some Incedents [sic] in the Life of J.F. Reed. It is not known when the manuscript was written. This fragment includes pages 30-59, Reed’s time at Iowa State Normal School, circa 1885. There is no record of when it came into the possession of Special Collections.

title: E.G. Miller’s “Beginnings of the Iowa Normal School”, 1904
description: Edward G. Miller was born in Wisconsin on September 3, 1840, and died in Iowa on May 30, 1906. He was a veteran of the Civil War, serving first with Company K., 1st Wisconsin Infantry Regiment. He later became the commanding officer of Company G., 20th Wisconsin Infantry Regiment. After moving to Iowa, he was elected state senator from Black Hawk County. It was Captain Miller who introduced the bill to establish the Iowa State Normal School. From the introduction to article: “Captain E. G. Miller, who was representing Black Hawk county in the Iowa state senate at the time Iowa State Normal school was established, was asked by the program committee for Old Settlers’ day to prepare a paper treating of the incidents surrounding the establishment of the school, which has become one of the most notable in the United States. Mr. Miller responded reluctantly, fearing his paper would be too much in the first person and smacking of egotism, but these feelings were overcome and we have herewith a very splendid resume of the history of the founding of the Normal school…” || This collection contains an article E.G. Miller wrote about Iowa State Normal School in 1904 and a letter from Captain Miller to Normal School President H.H. Seerley.

title: Audio Cassettes
description: Robert Beach – January 6, 1972 (1 cassette tape): Radio interview conducted by Mr. Herb Hake with Bob Beach, owner of the University Book and Supply, in Cedar Falls. The interview took place aboard the bookstore’s unique London double decker bus which served to transport students around the college hill area. The interview explains how and why the bus was purchased, how it was maintained, and the experience the ride provided. NOTE: This recording has been digitized in mp3 and WAV format and is available upon request. Rose Irene Maiden Bolstad – 1991 (9 cassette tapes): Narrations by musician Rose Irene Maiden Bolstad, a 1948 graduate of Iowa State Teachers College, recounting her time on campus. The tapes include detailed recollections of student life during the mid-twentieth century. Topics discussed include courses attended, professors, daily student life, musical training, community life, leisure activities, teaching, shopping, fashion, campus living, and dating. Tapes also include some narration by Mrs. Bolstad's sister. A detailed list of topics covered accompanies each tape. Priscilla Mae Cox with Rickie Lynn Cox – March 14, 1990 (1 cassette tape): Narration by Ms. Cox who was the first woman photographer in the state of Iowa. She was the photo artist for the early UNI yearbooks and was instrumental in persuading university president Constantine Curris to revive the yearbook. The tape also includes brief anecdotes about difficulties faced by teachers during the great depression by Sadie Cambell, the married student Quonset huts. Includes brief anecdotes on Oscar the alligator who once lived in the UNI greenhouse and George the skeleton who accompanied Rickie Lynn Cox to UNI football games and met the Governor of Iowa and the president of UNI. NOTE: This recording has been digitized in mp3 and WAV format and is available upon request. John Page – May 3, 1990 (1 cassette tape): Narration by John Page concerning the portrait of former UNI President Mauker. The narration includes; how the portrait was funded, the members of the selection committee (Page was the chair), the selection of the artist and terms of the agreement concerning the purchase of the portrait. The focus of the narration is the controversy the painting generated by Professor J. Fox who, in a letter to the College Eye, suggested that students and faculty purchase the portrait and burn it. The artist visited UNI to address the issue of burning works of art. NOTE: This recording has been digitized in mp3 and WAV format and is available upon request. Claud R. Wynegar – March 14, 1970 (4 cassette tapes): Claud R. Wynegar talks about the early history of Cedar Falls. Highlights from the interview include descriptions of: the Cedar Valley Fair auto races, Presidents Theodore Roosevelt and William Taft’s visits and speeches in Cedar Falls, and the only KKK meeting and cross burning in Cedar Falls. Stella Wynegar – August 15, 1970 (4 cassette tapes): Stella Wynegar interviewed by Herb Hake. Stella Wynegar was 91 at the time of the interview and discusses a multitude of topics about her life in Cedar Falls. Highlights from the interview include: her visit with Buffalo Bill Cody, early doctors in Cedar Falls, and history of early businesses, saloons (women were warned to stay away from this area), the Chinese laundry, and the opera house.
